# Answer key — Chapter 11: Resilience, RAID and backup {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-11-redundancy-raid · basic)* — **Correct: c.**
@def-raid states that RAID 5 (and RAID 6) distribute data with parity,
tolerating one (respectively two) failed disks; option a describes RAID 1,
option b describes RAID 0, and option d is nonsense (RAID combines physical
disks into one logical volume, not the reverse).

**Q2** *(tests @sec-11-redundancy-raid · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
The chapter's rule "RAID is not a backup": a mirror or parity array
instantly and exactly copies a deletion, corruption or ransomware
encryption to every disk, so only a point-in-time copy (a backup) allows a
return to an earlier state.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-11-backup · basic)* — **Correct: a.**
The 3–2–1 rule is three copies of important data, on two different kinds of
media, with one copy off-site (or, in the cloud, in a separate account or
region) — see @sec-11-backup. The other options confuse it with backup
schedules, RAID layouts and cloud geography.

**Q4** *(tests @sec-11-availability-revisited · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"one failure takes down as little as possible", "limiting how much a single
failure destroys" (any phrasing that names the design goal that a single
failure affects as little as possible), plus one example from the chapter:
spreading a deployment across availability zones, backing up data so the
loss of storage is survivable, or building from immutable images so a lost
instance is replaced.

**Q5** *(tests @sec-11-backup · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"a backup that has never been restored is not known to work", "an untested
backup is not a control", "restore testing proves the backup actually
works" (any phrasing that says the point of the backup is the restore, and
only testing the restore proves it works — CSA, 2024, p. 255).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-11-provider-redundancy · basic)* — **Correct: d.**
The chapter says deletion, corruption and ransomware reach through all
provider redundancy because replicas copy the damage as exactly as a RAID
array does; resilience is layered, and the customer's own backup remains the
customer's responsibility.

**Q7 — applied scenario** *(tests @sec-11-designing-for-failure · applied)* —
**Model answer:** (i) RAID 5 does not help: it mirrors/parity-copies the
encryption to every disk — RAID buys uptime through hardware failure, not
recoverability (@tbl-raidbackup). (ii) The snapshot is a rollback point but
sits in the same cloud account, so an attacker who can reach the account can
destroy or encrypt it too; the chapter warns it must not be mistaken for the
backup. (iii) The decisive control (@exm-backup-trc) is a regular backup of
Nextcloud's data and configuration that is *off-site* (separate account or
region — a backup the attacker can reach and encrypt is no backup, the
Session 10 off-host-logs logic), *immutable* (cannot be encrypted or deleted
by ransomware), and *tested by restoring on a schedule* (a backup that has
never been restored is not known to work). Grading notes: full credit needs
a correct helps/does-not-help verdict with a reason for all three
safeguards, plus all three backup properties each justified; partial credit
for naming the properties without tying each to the chapter's reasoning.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-11-resilience-vs-prevention)* Preventive controls reduce the
likelihood of a bad event (firewall, MFA, WAF); resilience accepts that
failures will occur and reduces their impact, so that the service keeps
running or recovers quickly.

(2) *(@exr-11-raid0-trap)* RAID 0 stripes data across disks for speed with
no redundancy, so any one disk failing destroys the whole array, making it
more likely to lose data than a single disk despite its place among the
redundant arrays.

(3) *(@exr-11-raid-not-backup)* RAID maintains a current copy, so it mirrors
any change, including harmful ones. It survives a disk failing; it does not
survive a file being deleted or corrupted, or ransomware encrypting the
data, all of which are replicated instantly to every disk.

(4) *(@exr-11-321-rule)* Three copies, on two media types, one off-site (or
a separate cloud account or region). The off-site copy matters because a
backup the attacker can reach can be encrypted too; the same logic as
shipping logs off-host in Session 10: a safeguard under the attacker's
control is no safeguard.

(5) *(@exr-11-data-loss-trc)* Threat: data lost through disk failure,
corruption, ransomware or accidental deletion. Risk: severe impact of
permanent loss; several causes not rare. Controls: RAID for hardware
failure, snapshots for rollback, and, as the one that guarantees recovery, a
regular, off-site, immutable backup that is tested by restoring it.
